Muscular layer: Muscular layer lies just below the epidermis. It consists of outer thin layer of circular muscle fibres (around the body) and inner thick layer of longitudinal muscle fibre (along the length of body). • Circular muscle layer is thin and contains scattered granules of porphyrin pigment which imparts brown colour to the skin. • Longitudinal muscle layer is thicker and lies in the form of parallel bundles separated by connective tissue and strengthened by collagen fibres. • There is another thin strip of circular muscle lying below the layer of longitudinal muscles. Circular muscles and longitudinal muscles are opposite in function i.e. contraction of one cause relaxation of other and vice versa.
4. Parietal coelomic epithelium: It is a thin and single layer of flattened squamous epithelial cells that forms the outer envelope of coelom.

Coelom in earthworm Earthworm has true coelom or schizocoel which is the cavity between alimentary canal and body wall and is formed by splitting of mesoderm in the embryonic stage. Coelom of earthworm is divided into a number of coelomic chambers by the intersegmental muscular septa. Septa are absent up to the 4th segment and present behind it. The first septum is thin and lying in between 4th and 5th segment. Similarly, there is only a single septum between 8th and 10th segments. Septa from 4th /5th upto 13th /14th are without perforations whereas septa from 14th /15th up to the last are with sphinctered openings.

Coelom in earthworm is filled with an alkaline, whitish or colourless fluid that contains salts, proteins, water and coelomic corpuscles. Coelomic corpuscles are of four types: i. Phagocytes or amoebocytes or granulocytes: They are the largest and more numerous cells. They are nucleated cells having amoeboid shape. They are called phagocytes since they eat/engulf bacteria. ii. Mucocytes: They are elongated cells which have broad fan like structure at one end and narrow nucleated part at the other end. iii. Circular nucleated cell: These cells are less numerous, round shaped, nucleated and filled with clear cytoplasm. iv. Chloragogen cell: They are star shaped and small sized cells. They become deep yellow coloured when stained in iodine solution. They are excretory in function and remove waste from coelomic fluid. They are analogous to the liver of higher animals as they store reserve food material in the form of glycogen.

It also acts as antiseptic protecting skin from microbial infection. 8.3.4 DIGESTIVE SYSTEM Let’s discuss the given questions.

i. What process actually occurs in the process of digestion? ii. Do earthworms have complete or incomplete alimentary canal? Why? iii. What is the feeding habit of earthworm? Digestive system is the complex system of organs chiefly concerned for the conversion of complex food particles into simpler forms by the action of digestive organs and digestive glands. This system also performs the absorption of nutrients from the digested food and elimination of undigested food particles in the form of faeces. Digestive system can be broadly divided into alimentary canal and digestive glands. Alimentary canal: In earthworm, it is a long, complete and straight tubular structure of varying diameter extending from mouth to anus; also called gastrointestinal tract. It consists of following parts:

Figure 8.3.8 Alimentary canal of Pheretima posthuma 1. Mouth and buccal chamber (1st - 3rd segment) : Mouth is the crescentic opening, lying below the prostomium at the ventral position in the first segment. It posteriorly leads into a short, narrow and thin walled protrusible chamber or cavity called buccal chamber. Buccal cavity extends up to the middle of 3rd segment. The innermost epithelial layer of buccal chamber is thrown into longitudinal folds.
